paras: The attempted lynching of John Dixon took place at Sparta, Hancock County, Georgia, on August 3, 1903, when a mob gathered to kill Dixon, a young Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and chased the sheriff who held him to the railroad depot. Sheriff Berry put Dixon on a train just before the mob's leaders arrived and lodged him in the Macon jail. A short Associated Press dispatch carried the story to white papers from Georgia to Massachusetts.

The accusation arose from an incident near Sparta on the night of Sunday, August 2, but the reports disagree about who the woman was. According to a Macon special printed in the Alexandria Gazette, Mrs. McLeon, "a prominent white lady of Sparta," went into her back yard to quiet a dog and was "set upon by the negro" as she returned to the house. The New-York Tribune's correspondent named her Mrs. Henry McLean, wife of one of the county's best-known planters, and wrote that she fainted after her cries frightened the man away.
The Associated Press version instead described the woman as the daughter of a farmer near Sparta, said her screams caused her attacker to desist, and reported that she was uninjured.

Mrs. McLeon's husband, away on business in Sparta, set out with a party of neighbors to find the man. Dixon was captured by Sheriff Berry, and on Monday morning the husband "made desperate efforts to shoot him, but was prevented." According to the wire report, Dixon was first held in the Sparta jail, but as a mob was forming the sheriff took him to the train.

The Tribune wrote that the husband's posse "went for reinforcements" while the sheriff made for Sparta, and that the train pulled out just as the leaders of the mob rode up. The Gazette's account called it "a race to the depot" that the sheriff won "by a small margin": the mob's leaders reached the station as Dixon was put aboard, and the conductor ordered the engineer ahead before they could act. Dixon, "heavily manacled," reached Macon at noon by the Atlanta Constitution's account, or in the afternoon by the wire's, and was lodged in the jail there. No paper reported that the mob or the husband injured him.
The reports end with Dixon held at Macon "for safe keeping"; no report of an indictment or trial for him, or of any action against members of the mob, appears in the coverage.

Most readers met the case in a short Associated Press dispatch dated Macon, August 3, which ran on August 4 and 5 in papers from Savannah, Montgomery and Birmingham to Richmond, Raleigh and Worcester. Headlines ranged from "SAVED BY HER CRIES" in Savannah and "SHERIFF SPIRITED NEGRO FROM MOB" in Richmond to "Same Old Story." in the Williamsburg Virginia Gazette, which reprinted the item on August 8.

The New-York Tribune printed its own telegram under the headline "TRIED TO KILL PRISONER. Sheriff Saves Negro from Man Whose Wife He Assaulted," stating the alleged assault as fact. The Alexandria Gazette ran the fullest account under a "LYNCH LAW FEVER" heading and wrote that the mob had gathered "to deal out swift justice to Mrs. McLeon's assailant." The opening of that account also ran in the Atlanta Constitution as "Negro Saved from Angry Mob," in a copy dated August 10.

The Newberry Herald and News of South Carolina condensed the case into one sentence on August 7, describing the woman as "a young white girl." Every account found was in a white paper; each identified Dixon only as "a negro," reported the charge in the reporter's own voice, and gave no statement from him.

The accounts disagree on the accuser: the Macon special and the Tribune, which share no wording, name a married woman, Mrs. McLeon or McLean, while the wire report describes a farmer's daughter and the Newberry paper "a young white girl." They also differ on the charge, given as assault in most accounts and as attempted assault in the Newberry item, and on Dixon's age, 20 in the wire report and seventeen in the Tribune.

bases: A mob formed at Sparta to kill John Dixon, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and chased the sheriff to the depot, but the sheriff got him to the Macon jail unharmed (A1, A2, A3, A10).

A mob gathered to deal 'swift justice' for an alleged assault and the husband tried to shoot Dixon, but no one was killed; Dixon reached the Macon jail (A1, A3, A10). It is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

Three accounts that do not share wording (the AP dispatch A2, the Tribune's own telegram A3, and the Macon special in A1/A12) agree that Sheriff Berry took Dixon from Sparta to the Macon jail ahead of a mob, though they differ on the accuser.

accounts.gist: Dixon, heavily manacled, was brought to Macon by Sheriff Berry after barely escaping an infuriated mob; the fuller version says Mrs. McLeon was attacked in her back yard Sunday night, her husband tried to shoot Dixon, and the sheriff won a race to the depot.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune correspondent
accounts.gist: Dixon, seventeen, was accused of assaulting Mrs. Henry McLean, who fainted; her husband tried to shoot him in the sheriff's hands, then the posse went for reinforcements and the sheriff's train left Sparta as the mob's leaders rode up.

framing.detail: The AP dispatch ran under headlines stressing the rescue or the charge: 'SAVED BY HER CRIES' (Savannah), 'SHERIFF SPIRITED NEGRO FROM MOB' (Richmond), 'Negro Charged With Assault' (Birmingham), 'Jailed for Attempted Assault' (Raleigh).

The Alexandria Gazette grouped the case under 'LYNCH LAW FEVER' and said the mob gathered 'to deal out swift justice' to the woman's 'assailant', stating the attack as fact while recounting the sheriff's escape.
The New-York Tribune headed its telegram 'TRIED TO KILL PRISONER. Sheriff Saves Negro from Man Whose Wife He Assaulted', treating the assault as established.
The Williamsburg Virginia Gazette reprinted the wire under the headline 'Same Old Story.', presenting the case as a familiar type.
